articleTitle: Solid State: VLSI: Some fundamental challenges: Defining and designing the products made possible by very-large-scale integration are first on the list of priority tasks
abstract: A tremendous interest in VLSI is all around us. There is much talk of electron-beam and X-ray lithography tools to achieve VLSI's submicron structures. In all of the discussions, the implication is that VLSI will allow us to enjoy the same kind of fantastic low-cost advantages that previous IC technologies have provided in electronic products. Perhaps. But if the semiconductor industry had today a commercial million-transistor technology like VLSI, I'm not so sure it would know what to do with it. Besides products containing memory devices, it isn't clear how future VLSI can be used in electronic products.

articleTitle: Memories: An optical disk replaces 25 mag tapes: This 30-cm disk features a long-life tellurium film upon which data is impressed by laser
abstract: The problem was to develop an inexpensive disk recorder of digital information. It was to have direct read-after-write capability and to be able to record in an ordinary room, not the usual clean room required for dust protection.

articleTitle: IV. `Hellman presents no shortcut solutions to the DES'
abstract: Prof. Martin Hellman presents no shortcut solutions to the Data Encryption Standard; the time-memory tradeoff is just one of many key-message exhaustion techniques. Therefore when he says, "DES is only marginally secure today and will be totally insecure within ten years," he is totally wrong.

articleTitle: The accident that shouldn't have happened: A narrative account of what is believed to have occurred, based on reports from many experts
abstract: A schematic of Three Mile Island Unit 2, opposite p. 42, will help you follow the sequence of numbered events that comprised the nuclear reactor accident. FOLD OUT this schematic before beginning the articles on this page. Then choose the article that best suits you — if you're not already familiar with the workings of pressurized water reactors, begin with the article directly below; but, if you are an expert in nuclear reactor systems, read John Mason's scenario.

articleTitle: Special issue: Three Mile Island and the future of nuclear power [special issue intro.]
abstract: This special issue will focus on the follwoing questions: What happened on the morning of March 28, 1979 at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania? What significance do those events take on when considered in the context of nuclear power plant safety? What bearing might those events have on the future use and development of nuclear power? and Who will determine nuclear power's future? These questions are tackled one by one. Their importance to all citizens is clear. But in gathering information for this issue, Spectrum's editors have become increasingly aware of the special challenge that the accident at Three Mile Island presents to electrical and electronics engineers.

articleTitle: Computers: Projecting VLSI's impact on microprocessors: Single-chip microcomputers with 1 million bits of information, English-language programming, and canned software are seen ahead
abstract: One million devices on a single silicon chip by 1985? RAMS of 1024 kbits with prices as low as 0.002 cent per bit? Both developments will be possible in the next decade with a new generation of very-large-scale integrated circuits. Microprocessors and related components will be built on these ICS with new circuit-design techniques and advanced fabrication processes. Among the likely products are single-chip microcomputers with as much as 256 kbits of electrically erasable memory.

articleTitle: Microprocessors: The amazing micromice: See how they won: Probing the innards of the smartest and fastest entries in the Amazing Micro-Mouse Maze Contest
abstract: The stage was set. A crowd of spectators, mainly engineers, were there. So were reporters from the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times, other publications, and television. All waited in expectancy as Spectrum's Mystery Mouse Maze was unveiled. Then the color television cameras of CBS and NBC began to roll; the moment would be recreated that evening for viewers of the Walter Cronkite and John Chancellor-David Brinkley news shows. The final races of the Amazing Micro-Mouse Maze Contest were beginning at the National Computer Conference in New York, and what was perhaps most amazing was the wide public interest that the competition had evoked almost since its inception.

articleTitle: Control: Practical magnetic bearings: Electronically controlled electromagnets support spinning 1100-kg shafts to micrometer accuracy
abstract: The suspension of a rotating shaft in a magnetic field without mechanical contact or lubrication is an old idea. But now, with advanced electronic control, a magnetically suspended 1100-kg shaft capable of spinning at 10 00 r/min or even higher is becoming a commercial reality. Already such shafts, turning at various speeds, are being used in grinding and polishing machinery, vacuum pumps, compressors, turbines, generators, and centrifuges.

articleTitle: Communications: On foiling computer crime: Can a thief with lots of LSI chips crack present data scrambling schemes? The experts debate the matter
abstract: In the following series of articles, three well-known cryptographers and two U.S. Government agencies again do battle on the question of whether the federally approved Data Encryption Standard (DES) will be secure against commercial data thefts for the next five or ten years.

articleTitle: Marine/aviation: Omega: Global navigating by VLF fix: This internationally sponsored global VLF system is nearing full operational status
abstract: Omega is shaping up as the only system that meets the world's need in the rest of this century for simple, economical, moderately accurate navigation by sea and air. Now nearing full operational status, this VLF system will provide worldwide, all-weather position fixes with root-mean-square accuracy of 1-2 nautical miles. The minimum receiver cost is perhaps the lowest of any navigation system - just a few thousand dollars. Thanks to steady increases in microprocessor applications, a user just enters initial position, and the system can continuously read out positions anywhere on the globe.

articleTitle: Telephones go digital: Lower cost, higher performance and greater flexibility favor the digital approach over analog switching
abstract: It is only a matter of time before the largely analog telephone system becomes all-digital. One big reason is cost. Devices like microprocessors, memory, and logic are now no more expensive than analog devices. Another reason is performance. Digital switching networks are easier to maintain than analog; they have fewer components for higherreliabilitylevels, require less floor space, dissipate less power and are easier to install. In addition they can handle more traffic per equipment frame and provide uniform transmission capabilities, Yet a third big reason is versatility. When put into digital form, information from a variety of sources-video, audio, and facsimile-can be multiplexed and transmitted over conventional and coaxial cable, radio waves, and other media. Digital information can also be easily coded for privacy, a must for such modern telecommunications services as electronic funds transfer.

articleTitle: Transportation: A green light for advanced train controls: Solid-state developments yield hands-off operation of second-generation systems
abstract: Train control systems have been around for more than 100 years, but only relatively recently — with advances in semiconductor and computer technology — has it been possible to talk of new generations of equipment. With the second generation has come the automated operation of trains, including their starting, stopping, opening and closing of doors, and maintaining of speed. Wayside central computers integrate and stabilize the overall system. The third generation of controls is under development and should be in revenue service by 1980. It will use microprocessors on board the train and in stations to provide greater flexibility of control, increased reliability, and superior service for passengers.

articleTitle: I. The 64-kbit RAM: A prelude to VLSI
abstract: The 64-kbit dynamic random-access memory may signal the end of the MOS transistor era. Established process technology and manufacturing techniques will no longer do; the new RAM demands a quantum jump beyond them. It is a prelude to very large-scale integration (VLSI), or the placing of more than 100 000 logic gates on a single chip.

articleTitle: Education: Accelerating the practice of engineering
abstract: Considers the course structure of engineering students at the Harvey Mudd College, Los Angeles. The author explains that the students must complete at least a third of their curricular programme in the humanities and social sciences, the aim being to `humanise' engineers. An integral part of this engineering course is the design engineering phase where teams of three or four undergraduates undertake professional design and development projects for industry and government, which helps in giving them an insight to industry.

articleTitle: III. `Hellman's scheme breaks DES in its basic form'
abstract: The time-memory tradeoff scheme of Prof. Martin E. Hellman, for practical purposes, breaks DES in its present basic form. It should be pointed out, though, that a time-memory tradeoff can be used to break any block ciphers that have similar key lengths and can reduce deciphering time by a significant factor.

Years of industrial robot development, refinements, and improvements are beginning to pay off. The industrial robot, a programmed manipulator designed to work atuomatically, is becoming as much a part of a manufacturing plant as a punch press or drilling machine. Its integration into many machining centers and production lines has been so smooth that it is hardly distinguishable from the vast machines it works with side by side, save for its moving appendages.

articleTitle: Power: Electrical load management: The British experience: Reduced utility rates and heaters with storage have been increasing winter off-peak loads
abstract: Britain's two decades of success with load management — techniques to smooth out the peaks and valleys in consumer use of electricity — can benefit other parts of the world where there is uneconomical use of energy. Using energy storage on the customer's premises for the heating of space and water, along with rates that encourage off-peak use of electricity, the British have eliminated peak power demand on winter mornings and increased the use of electricity at night, when the demand is low.

articleTitle: LSI yields high reliability: Cost and size of telephone-interface equipment shrinks, while IC designs displace electromechanical versions
abstract: Semiconductor technology in the telephone industry is having its greatest impact on switching equipment. This is having far-reaching implications for both the telephone industry and the semiconductor industry. On the one hand, telephone switching equipment promises to become smaller, cheaper, more reliable, and less costly to maintain. It will make it possible to offer more services. On the other hand, the semiconductor manufacturer must change his way of thinking from that of a component supplier to that of a subsystems supplier. He must be aware of the functions his products will perform in the customer's equipment.

articleTitle: V. `Hellman's data does not support his conclusion'
abstract: Neither the information obtained by the National Bureau of Standards nor the discussions in Prof. Martin Hellman's paper support his conclusion that the Data Encryption Standard will likely be "totally insecure within ten years."

articleTitle: Power/energy: No ill winds for New Mexico utility: Under test in one municipality's power system, an experimental machine supplies up to 15 percent of community needs
abstract: It has been a little more than a year since the first Federally sponsored large wind generator joined the electric utility system in the town of Clayton, N.M., and while much remains to be studied, already it is clear: the results are encouraging. Linked to the town's present system of seven diesel generators, the revolving wind blades can supply 200 kW of output power, nearly 15 percent of Clayton's total power load during off-peak periods.

articleTitle: 100000+ gates on a chip: mastering the minutia. II. Needed: a `miracle slice' for VLSI fabrication
abstract: Very large scale integration (VLSI) is perhaps the decade's most eagerly anticipated microelectronics revolution. Promised is an era of computational plenty: machine intelligence made practical by qualitative computation carried out at low cost. No longer need designers be guided by "conservation of hardware" dogma, which has held sway since computers were invented.

articleTitle: Three systems defined: Advanced satellite and microwave radio techniques will facilitate gigabit per second capacities
abstract: A new generation of digital data-transmission services in the coming decade could change the ways business is conducted. Using all available earth and space technologies, large corporations are setting up ventures for nationwide datacommunications networks. Three of the more promising ventures will be competing directly for the business dollar. They include one service from a consortium called Satellite Business Systems, a three-way partnership formed by the IBM Corp., Comsat General Corp., and Aetna Life and Casualty Co.; another service, the Xerox Telecommunications Network, from the Xerox Corp.; the Advanced Communications Service, and a scanning-beam satellite system service, both from the American Telephone & Telegraph Co. (AT&T).

articleTitle: I. U.S. and Canada: Initial results reported
abstract: Limited operation of commercial optical-waveguide communication links in the United States and Canada has turned up at least one unexpected result: Some subscribers were unnerved when they used the links. The lack of electrical noise in the circuit seemed to confuse them. An optical system, of course, eliminates several sources of noise, yielding a circuit that is unusually quiet.

articleTitle: Nuclear power around the world: Where the plants are located and a country-by-country projection showing nuclear's part in total electric energy production
abstract: Three Mile Island Unit 2 has become the reactor heard round the world. The accident has shaken confidence in Europe and the Far East in nuclear safety - more in the public's mind, of course, than in the minds of nuclear-power scientists and engineers - and planning for safety has been tightened. It has not deterred the commitments of most nations to nuclear power, but in some countries the issue has become a thorny political one.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Solar Power Satellite: Putting it together: Enormous structures involving unique fabrication methods call for new materials, tools, and heavy-lift vehicles
abstract: Building a Solar Power Satellite in space is not an easy feat. Consider the following: • It will be necessary to put up an assembly line in space. • Lightweight, but at the same time strong and durable, materials will be needed. • There are specific advantages to each of the two options on where in space to build the SPS: directly in geosynchronous orbit (GEO), or in low earth orbit. (LEO), with subsequent transfer to GEO. • A completely new heavy-lift launch vehicle will be needed to carry the construction equipment and materials aloft. • Special manipulative tools will be required for assembly work in space.

articleTitle: The wired household: Teletext services pave the way for a variety of useful monitoring and control features in the home
abstract: Information retrieval is not the only capability that advanced electronics can offer to households. Other, more complex chores can be performed by specialized terminals that combine microprocessors with relatively conventional hardware. Three experimental systems now in the laboratory would do the following in homes: 1. Control the use of electricity to avert overloading at utilities that can lead to blackouts. 2. Turn the television receiver into a programmable information/entertainment center. 3. Use the telephone at idle times for meter reading, alarm reporting, and the remote monitoring and control of lighting, heating, and air-conditioning.

articleTitle: Sociotechnology: Microwave hazards: Are U.S. standards for safe exposure levels adequate? One IEEE member warns of smug complacency; another responds
abstract: What is the truth about microwave hazards? The publication in 1977 of The Zapping of America: Microwaves, Their Deadly Risk, attracted much attention throughout the United States, particularly within the electronics industry, because it was heralded by its publicists as a major expose of the dangers of microwave radiation - dangers “hidden from you by the Pentagon, the State Department, and the electronics industry.” Lending apparent credibility to the book, which was published by W. W. Norton, was the fact that it was written by Paul Brodeur and based on two articles by him in The New Yorker (Dec. 13 and 20, 1976). The author, an award-winning science writer, had previously written about the asbestos and vinyl-chloride industries.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics. Higher fi by digits: Digitally encoded audio disks and associated playback gear promise breakthrough in high fidelity, low noise
abstract: In the early 1980s, manufacturers will begin marketing systems that produce high fidelity sound from digitally encoded audio disks. The sound, as contrasted with that from analog audio disks, will have increased maximum dynamic range and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and no tracking distortion, wow, flutter, pop or surface noise. Demonstration systems have been impressive, and the total lack of background noise of any kind during pauses in musical passages is particularly dramatic.

articleTitle: Engineering ethics: How to be ethical and survive: Some engineering societies offer aid in a conflict, but competence and confidence can help mitigate trauma and duress
abstract: Engineers sometimes find that attempts to practice their profession ethically can lead to conflicts with their managers. Where such conflicts have involved the public safety, dramatic confrontations have resulted. Here are well-known examples: • In 1972 in San Francisco, a Bay Area Rapid Transit train overran a station and plowed into a sandpile. Immediately questions were raised publicly about the safety of the new system's automatic features. The accident was traced to a crystal oscillator in an operating subsystem that had transmitted the wrong speed to the train. Costly corrective retrofitting and a backup system were ordered, but critics said there were design flaws that should have been caught before the railroad line was built. • In 1974a Turkish Airlines DC-10 crashed nine minutes after takeoff from Paris when the jet's rear cargo door flew off at 13 000 feet. The sudden decompression crushed the cabin floor and the plane's hydraulic steering apparatus. In all, 346 persons died. Again, a public controversy erupted, with critics charging that the builders of the craft and even the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration knew that the door design was defective. The latching mechanism and the omission of floor venting were problems that could have been corrected at low cost when recognized during the design phase. The cost rose steeply as designs were converted to production processes and then to airplanes.

articleTitle: Instrumentation: Ingenuity abounds: Trends: In-field diagnostics, in-plant and in-process testing, and smarter portables
abstract: They are labeled logic state analyzers, timing analyzers, multitesters, signature analyzers, and in-circuit emulators, and they have one thing in common: they diagnose electronic-equipment faults rapidly. Service troubleshooters with only a minimum of training use them to make repairs in the field (Fig. 1). These diagnostic instruments have been made “smart” by microprocessor technology. This is one trend in instrumentation.

articleTitle: Electronics in medicine: The microprocessor takes over and the ultimate CAT scanner nears completion, but costs still soar
abstract: Last September a report from the United States Office of Technology Assessment called for new ways to evaluate the efficacy and safety of medical technologies, as well as their cost effectiveness and social impacts. Shortly thereafter Joseph Califano Jr., Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, told the annual meeting of the Institute of Medicine that his department was concerned about allegedly extravagant use of advanced medical technology. It was, in some respects, a year of seeming contradictions for medical electronics.

articleTitle: Education: Equipment shortfall in EE labs: Undergraduate schools for the most part have substandard, obsolete equipment and it's in short supply, too
abstract: Hunched over test instruments in a laboratory, with a scientific calculator within reach, undergraduates at the University of Colorado School of Engineering are a picture of rapt learning. But there is something wrong with the picture. The students are studying modern integrated-circuit technology, but the school's test instruments — a signal generator, an oscilloscope, an impedance bridge — are all vacuum-tube relics from the late 1950s. The calculator is new, but it is not school property; it belongs to one of the students.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Solar Power Satellite ground stations: The ground systems for microwave beaming from the SPS would require a rectifying antenna with over 13 billion elements
abstract: Picture a low-gain rectifying antenna that is about 10 km in diameter, consists of 13 billion elements and has seven billion rectifiers. Add a medium-voltage dc power-collecting grid, dc/ac converters, and a high-voltage ac power-collecting grid. What you have roughly is the main ground installation for the Solar Power Satellite (SPS) system, and its immensity is almost overpowering. Yet studies done for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration and the Federal Department of Energy indicate that the size and complexity of the equipment are not beyond present capabilities for production and construction.

articleTitle: Sociotechnology: Science, technology, and the human condition: The impact of science and engineering on citizens is great, despite their questionable impact on social institutions
abstract: While technology has been clearly beneficial to many people, it has been of dubious value in improving man's social condition. Government, personal, and family relations are not better — and may even have deteriorated — since the advent of sophisticated technologies. What follows is a broad overview of science and technology-directed change in the human condition in the United States. The intent is not to be exhaustive but rather to stimulate thought and debate.

Progress in low-loss optical-fiber technology, including both device fabrication and transmission equipment, is so advanced in Japan that such systems are considered practical for several commercial applications. Experience has been gained with optical waveguide systems in public communications, video transmission, data links, and electric power control.

articleTitle: Finances: How inflation affects your retirement dollar: At 13 percent annual inflation, an annual living expense of $24 000 in 1979 dollars will soar to $323 000 in 20 years
abstract: Most engineers are as concerned and baffled about continuing inflation as economists are. There are many plausible explanations for inflation but still no successful remedies. Working engineers — particularly young engineers — tend to accept inflation with the knowledge that their earned incomes will reflect the depreciation of the dollar. In other words, their incomes will be indexed to the inflation rate. Their tendency is to put off saving and to accelerate spending, since an unspent dollar won't be as valuable in the future.

Very-large-scale integration (VLSI) is seen as the raw material needed for a quantum jump in the exploitation of electrotechnology. It will drive the microprocessor to new levels of performance! and the microprocessor, in turn, will extend itself into many `hitherto unimagined′ areas of application.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Opinions on nuclear power
abstract: In an ABC News-Harris survey conducted in May, 52 percent of the general public said they favored nuclear power plants, and 42 percent said they did not. In contrast, a poll by Spectrum of IEEE members in the U.S. conducted at about the same time showed 83 percent of those responding favoring the further development and use of nuclear power, while 13 percent said they did not, and four percent did not respond to that question. However, many who told Spectrum they favored nuclear power did so with qualifications. Among the most frequently listed qualifications were requirements for better safety systems and a concern for nuclear waste disposal.

“How depressing it is to think that the advance of technology is in the hands of the press and the politicians.” So said an engineer with the Magnavox Government Electronics Co. when Spectrum queried him on his reaction to coverage by the general news media of the Three Mile Island nuclear accident.

articleTitle: Office automation: A challenge: Better tools simplify some office tasks, but serious problems block the integrated office of the future
abstract: Upcoming communications services, to be made available with new commercial satellite and microwave systems, will greatly accelerate the drive toward the fully automatic “office of the future.” The concept received impetus from the introduction of word/text processors in the mid-1970s, but so far the average office continues to operate with a potpourri of mechanized tools but no integrated automated system. The efficiency of isolated tasks has been improved perhaps, but there has been little dramatic effect on productivity.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Nuclear power: The Swedish experience
abstract: Events at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania have drastically altered the activities and viewpoint of all parties with an interest in nuclear power: the utilities, regulatory bodies, the news media, and the general public. The ramifications of the nuclear accident will be explored in a future issue of Spectrum. Meanwhile it is interesting to note the impact of the event on one country: Sweden. In some respects, the history of nuclear power in Sweden represents a microcosm of events in all advanced nations.

articleTitle: Strategic arms control: SALT II: A state-of-the-art treaty: Compliance must be verifiable by technical means, so technology determines the treaty's leeway and its restrictions
abstract: After more than six years of negotiations for a second strategic arms-limitation treaty (SALT II), the United States and the Soviet Union may be close to an agreement. Hopes in Washington had been high for an initial handshake by May — “We expect this before May,” was the way Spurgeon Keeny, Deputy Director of the U.S. Arms Control and Disarmament Agency, had put it at a conference in Washington, D.C. -- but at this writing a new snag was looming over the issue of multiple warheads for Soviet missiles.

The events at Reactor Unit 2 on Three Mile Island have had a profound impact on Japan, where a firm commitment to nuclear power makes that nation second only to the United States in the use of nuclear energy. From the earliest hours of the Three Mile Island accident, the Japanese Government and utilities have been deeply involved in seeking to apply the lessons learned.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Electrical load management: The British experience, part II: Local and remote controls coupled with off-peak rates have forced nighttime demand to record highs
abstract: Load management has become a critical balancing act for power utilities. Consumer demand for electricity is, in general, rising as more and more power-driven equipment becomes part of the residential "good life" and a necessity for industry. Consumer use of electricity, however, is flawed by peaks and valleys that strain the generating capacity of power plants. The problem for utilities is: How can these peaks and valleys be smoothed out? In Britain, three systems have contributed to two decades of national success with load management:

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Personal and plentiful: Optical video disks debut in market tests; in the wings are digital audio, AM stereo, and flat screen TV
abstract: The incredible pace of new product innovation and introduction in consumer electronics continues unabated. Consider these recent developments: test-marketing of an optical video disk player in Atlanta; public demonstrations of digital audio systems with dynamic range in excess of 90 dB; prototype flat-screen television sets that are 100 percent solid state; educational toys that “talk back,” prompting children to learn a simple vocabulary; radio-controlled race cars for less than $10; and microprocessors in everything from gas stoves to ski boots.

The insistence by certain modern-day philosophers that we live in a “Chicken Little” world is overdrawn, but the exaggeration surely contains a degree of truth. Why is this? Those of conservative bent “ frequently members of the “establishment” - are traditionally inclined toward caution where risks are involved. But evidence of the trend is seen in liberal camps as well. It is apparent in the institutionalization of discontent that manifests itself in anti-technology movements.

articleTitle: The microcomputer invades the production line
abstract: There's a quiet revolution going on in the manufacturing world that is slowly changing the look of the factory floor. Spearheaded by mini- and microcomputer technologies, electronics is controlling and monitoring processes far more efficiently and quietly than clangy electromechanical relays - and with minimum human supervision.

articleTitle: Technology and society: Action on the international telecommunications front; the latest in energy R&D; agriculture goes electronic
abstract: How we communicate with one another, how we do business, how we entertain ourselves, what we learn about the world around us, whether we make war or peace — all come close to being dominated by the electronics technology available to us.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Computers to fight hijackers
abstract: The Federal Aviation Administration hopes somehow to automate the daily screening of three million passenger baggage items for bombs, firearms, and other threats. But the computing power required seems beyond that of present MOS microprocessors and even bipolar array computers.
Varying the speed of large industrial motors that drive pumps and compressors is basically a mechanical operation performed with valves and dampers that suppress the speed of the motor at its output.

articleTitle: International trade: Japan's electronics markets: A pair of views: Some denigrate dumping practices; others say the U.S. and other countries must learn how to compete
abstract: Japanese electronic products, most particularly in the consumer area, are proliferating in the U.S. market. Where U.S. corporations make competing products, prices have been driven down as a direct result of the Japanese challenge. This may make the U.S. consumer happy, but in some cases, U.S. companies have gone out of business, and this has put people out of work.

Although the world's telecommunications networks are going digital, the changeover from analog is occurring gradually. It would be impractical and prohibitively expensive to attempt to retire the present largely analog telephone network overnight and replace it with a digital one. Digital systems are being phased into existing installations with minimum interruption of subscriber services and the least inconvenience.

articleTitle: Optical systems: A review: Fiber-optics applications include power monitoring, video transmission, data links, and public communications
abstract: The advantages of fiber-optic communications have been demonstrated by experimental optical waveguide systems throughout the world. Among the important features stimulating research and development in fiber-optical communications are these: • Low transmission loss (greater distance between repeaters). • Wide transmission bandwidth. • Potential low cost. • Insensitivity to electromagnetic and radio-frequency interference. • Improved security compared with electronic cabling (no cross-talk among parallel cables). • Relatively small size, light weight, high strength, and flexibility. • Elimination of combustion or sparks caused by short circuits. • Flexibility in upgrading system capacity without need to install new cables. • Immunity to ground-loop problems. • Suitability for digital communications and pulsemodulation methods (fiber-optic cable losses are independent of transmission frequency). • Fewer government regulatory difficulties (because of the elimination of frequency allocation). • Suitability for relatively high temperature.

Huge expansion of nuclear power capacity - so huge that some observers might view it as unrealistic - is planned by the Soviet Union and seven Eastern Bloc countries. The goal is total installed capacity of 150 GW by 1990. The ambition of this plan can be measured by the previous target - 30 GW by 1980, a total that is not likely to be met. Present operating capacity is estimated at 16 GW, with some nuclear power stations due to go into operation in the next year or two.

articleTitle: Where do we go from here?: Analysis by the experts reveals steps to be undertaken in nuclear plant design, operating procedures, and institutional matters
abstract: Three Mile Island triggered at least six separate official investigations of the accident, and many more ad hoc studies. Indeed, an engineer at Babcock & Wilcox, builder of the TMI nuclear system, observed that analyzing the event had become the “new cottage industry” in the U.S.

Early design requirements for the Space Shuttle dictated a wingspan of 23.77 m, which reduced the aerodynamic stability of the 68 038.5-kg vehicle. To maintain stable flight in a vehicle that size, reactions to twisting, bending, flexing or other aerodynamic instabilities must be made in milliseconds-an impossible feat for humans. An all-digital electronic system was devised to compensate for the Shuttle's instability.

articleTitle: On Bell: II. The system is sound: `It ain't broke, so don't fix it,' reflects the sentiments of an eminent Bell Labs emeritus executive
abstract: Breaking up the Bell System in a way that I regard as arbitrary would make it harder, rather than easier, to harness new technology to the service of users. At present, telecommunications switching and transmission, information processing, and communication are all going digital. Unified development of this common technology would be the most efficient path to follow, not fragmented development through an enforced diversity of sources.

articleTitle: New product applications: 1-MBd modems link microcomputers and minicomputers at up to 10 440 m over coaxial cable
abstract: The Megalink family of high-speed coaxial-cable modems interconnects, without need for repeaters, microcomputer and minicomputer systems over distances up to 15 240 m, depending on the data rate and the type of cable used. They are intended for point-to-point, as well as multi-drop party-line operations, in either synchronous or asynchronous modes.

articleTitle: Electronics: Experts probe world outlook: Representatives of the world's nations review trends as the VLSI era approaches
abstract: The need to extend silicon semiconductor technology, particularly as the VLSI era dawns, was stressed recently by an international panel of engineers and executives representing most of the world's industrialized nations. The occasion was an ELECTRO '79 panel session in New York City, “An electronics executive forum on worldwide problems and opportunities.”

articleTitle: A Osborne & associates: An introduction to Microcomputers: Volume 2 and volume 3 there's nothing else like them
Communications. On the Bell System: Boom or `bust’? For all it's done for communications and the economy, its critics recommend its breakup
abstract: The restructuring of the American telecommunication industry and regulatory relationships is a complex matter. But restructuring is essential, argues Walter Hinchman, former Chief of the Common Carrier Bureau of the Federal Communications Commission. As he sees it, a U.S. telecommunications industry that has become firmly monopolistic under American Telephone and Telegraph threatens an increasingly information-based society. Mr. Hinchman proposes to break up the telecommunications industry into four distinct, competitive markets.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Data load: Wheat vs. chaff
abstract: Viewers of the CBS Television News show “60 minutes” were treated recently to a segment describing the U.S. businessman's plight in keeping up with the proliferating paperwork required by Government regulations. Several points were made: Federal agencies often require the same data, presented independently and in different formats; Federal, state, and regional governments require similar data, presented independently; and the time and money required by the businessman to report such data add up to a significant percentage of his business expense, and it is increasing.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Pocket interpreter breaks communication impasse
abstract: Tourists traveling abroad need no longer wind up with phrases that sound like “Where is the inkwell of my aunt?” when asking directions to the nearest lavatory. Lexicon Corp., a Miami-based electronics concern, has introduced a hand-held language microcomputer to assist the tourist.

articleTitle: Communications and microwave technology: The communications giants vie for interconnect turf; fiber optics go on-line; teletext is tested
abstract: Communications continues to be a field where new trends are as much a creature of politics as technology. In recent months, giant corporations like AT&T, Xerox, IBM, and RCA have all announced extensive — and overlapping — plans to meet tomorrow's business communications and data processing needs. Official information about some of these plans is sketchy, and must be gleaned or inferred, for the moment, from lengthy petitions for rule-making submitted to the Federal Communications Commission. Of particular interest are documents describing AT&T's proposed Advanced Communications Service, RCA's plans for a third geostationary Satcom satellite, and Xerox's request to set up a nationwide broadband digital network to be called the Xerox Telecommunications Network.

articleTitle: International technology: Japan turns its ingenuity to the world computer market: Breakthroughs in component design and system performance, along with finely honed marketing skills, underlie the Japanese challenge
abstract: The year 1978 will go down in history as the one in which the Japanese computer industry became a force to be reckoned with in world markets. After two decades of intensive development, Japan's leading mainframe makers unveiled in January 1978 what was heralded as the world's largest and fastest computer system. Then, before IBM could riposte, Fujitsu and Hitachi went on to announce in September that they would soon have available a system of even higher performance.

articleTitle: Electronics on wings, wheels, and waves: More speed and more safety through microprocessors, sensors, and advanced communications
abstract: By land, by air, and by sea, transportation systems are being invaded and improved by electronics as never before. Take the automobile. Systems with microcomputers are being designed to control the engine fuel pump, fuel injection, and ignition coil. Microcomputers are already offered as an option in luxury cars for the display and diagnosis of engine and vehicle parameters (see November 1978, pp. 30-35). Elsewhere a sampling of research and development projects in 1978 turns up such sophisticated equipment as this:

History records periods of great change with labels: Renaissance, Age of Reason, Industrial Revolution, and the like. The 20th century has ushered in the Electronic Revolution, and with it has come yet another label: the Information Society. Information management and exploitation, the experts say, will change the fabric of society. Manipulated by microelectronic, computer, radio, and other electronic disciplines, information has become a commodity on a par with pork bellies at the trade exchange. But unlike the prices of most commodities today, the price for exchange of information is decreasing because of electronics.

articleTitle: Solid state: 100 000+ gates on a chip: Mastering the minutia: The submicron geometries needed for VLSI have put IC makers on a new learning curve; object, to perfect feature delineation techniques
abstract: Semiconductor manufacturers are within sight of sub-micron feature sizes in their quest for ever more device density. Solid evidence of this fact can be found in the 64-kbit dynamic random access memory and 16-bit microcomputer already on the market. This two-part report describes first how fabrication techniques and production methods have changed to allow increased chip complexity. Next it outlines the tasks remaining to be done before 100 000 gates per chip, or more, become commonplace.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Progress in efficiency and reliability: Advances are defined in time-of-day rates, generation and transmission research, and protective systems
abstract: Greater efficiency from generating and transmission equipment, more effective use of power by consumers, and new methods for preventing power failures were major goals of the electric power industry in 1978. And they will remain goals for some time to come.

“Nuclear Nightmare” was the headline on Time magazine's cover following the Three Mile Island accident: Both the Pennsylvania event and the reaction of the news media to it sharpened the public's concern about — and, perhaps, its sensitivity to — the realities of risk and risk taking.

Participants in a recent forum on risk/benefit analysis, cosponsored by U.S. Senate and House subcommittees on science and technology and the American Association for the Advancement of Science, flirted with an interesting concept. Although it was not reduced to specific terms, it nevertheless seemed to hover, awaiting explication. The idea is this: Most, if not all, of the public's general distrust of science and technology relates to the hazards and risks associated therewith. Furthermore the public has difficulty categorizing risks and comparing one risk against another. Finally, if the public can be aided in categorizing and comparing risks, a great amount of the skepticism about technology will be dissipated and a wiser and more efficient application of technology to societal needs will ensue.

Communication system designs are moving toward a highly distributed control environment. Repetitive functions, such as digit or character processing, will be accomplished by “front end” microprocessors while file management and overall system control is performed by “rear end” processors. These two processing levels will be interconnected by an operating system spanning both processor levels and by fast communications hardware. This highly distributed processing environment requires communications software to be processor-transparent, thereby permitting processors and microprocessors to communicate efficiently and permitting a single software function to span both types of machines.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Spectrum: A progress report
abstract: A few years ago the staff of Spectrum undertook a redesign of the magazine to make it more useful to its readers. In particular, we increased the number of articles, decreased their average length, went to great lengths to avoid obscure mathematical expressions and to convert other mathematics to words reflecting their physical equivalents, and labored over illustrations to an extent not previously considered practical. We also began to take greater pains in selecting articles and the mix of articles in each issue. The positive feedback from readers confirmed that those judgments were appropriate. In more recent months we've added new departments to Spectrum: EEs' Tools and Toys, Engineer at large, and Best bits. All the while we have encouraged feedback through a variety of techniques — letters to Forum, the Reader Service card, and reader research conducted by independent firms, to name but three. Such feedback has increased dramatically, and the staff is encouraged and inspired by it. While it is not our practice to publish letters of praise in Forum, the following excerpts from reader correspondence may suggest some of the flavor of such letters.

articleTitle: The profession: The secret society that never was: Founded in the fires of creative disagreement, Eta Kappa Nu soon found its niche, and this month celebrates its 75th anniversary
abstract: On Sept. 23, 1904, two students at the University of Illinois met on the steps of the campus engineering building to discuss forming Eta Kappa Nu, the national electrical engineering honor society. One of the students, Maurice L. Carr, later recalled that their one enthusiastic agreement had been that such a society was needed; their views on exactly what the organization would achieve varied widely. Two days later, this time in front of University Hall, Carr and his colleagues, by then numbering five, agreed to form the association.

Trial optical-fiber communication systems operating in Europe in the last year have given telecommunication engineers greater confidence in the technical and economic feasibility of such systems. They note almost universal achievement of long repeater separations, early installation, and reliable operation. Operation of optical communication links at 8Mb/s and 34 Mb/s and 140 Mb/s appears practical. The next few years will see many more fully engineered systems carrying traffic while under evaluation.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: No way to run a railroad
abstract: It carries one-quarter of all the railroad commuters in the U.S., nearly 100 000 daily — a figure soon to be surpassed as ridership continues to increase. It is the famous and infamous and much maligned Long Island Rail Road. The Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) system, by comparison, moves 35 000 commuters daily.

articleTitle: The politics of technology. National Academy of Engineering: Is it merely an honorary society or does it have clout on Capitol Hill? A report on what it is and what it could be
abstract: In the 15 years since the National Academy of Engineering was established as part of the century-old National Academy of Sciences, the engineering group has grown and seemingly prospered. On paper it is part of the apparatus for advising the Federal Government on scientific and technical matters. Election to membership in the National Academy of Engineering _ which in 1979 was composed of 950 U.S. citizens and 74 foreign associates _ is widely recognized as a badge of professional achievement.

articleTitle: Management: Learning to live with red tape: It can tie up projects unduly, yet the organization man (or woman) can use it wisely
abstract: Do you hate red tape? Do you consider it a point of honor to frustrate it, bypass it or simply ignore it? If you do, you have lots of company — and most of you are probably heading for a great fall. If you think, “I could run this organization better and without the red tape,“ read on.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Looking back to look ahead
abstract: “What's past is prologue” is sufficiently timeworn to qualify as a cliche; yet it is a valid reminder that technical progress is more often made in a continuum and that real breakthroughs are rare. It serves also to discourage us from attempting to reinvent the wheel, and encourages us to exploit history in making technological projections and forecasts.

It was hailed as the most comprehensive study ever undertaken on reactor safety. Known variously as the Reactor Safety Study, WASH-1400, and the Rasmussen Report, the project involved a team of 60 persons, plus consultants, 70 man-years of effort, and some $4 million (see Spectrum, August 1975, pp. 46-55). During a review of the draft report, 1800 pages of comments were received from 87 individuals.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Teacher's PET talks to logic analyzer
abstract: Capt. David Smyth of the U.S. Army Signal Corps has come up with an interactive program to make a logic analyzer “invisible” to students operating it.

articleTitle: VLSI and other solid-state devices: New fabrication technologies put us on the threshold of a quantum jump in IC complexity
abstract: Hopes for advancement in semiconductor-chip density and complexity beyond present large-scale-integration (LSI) levels received a major boost last year. Fabrication techniques — ever the key to future integrated circuits — advanced to the point where semiconductor manufacturers are now within sight of a long sought goal: achievement of submicrometer feature sizes on a monolithic integrated circuit (IC)thereby providing a key capability for approaching the ultimate limits in IC complexity.

articleTitle: Aerospace and military: Progress in space structure research, aircraft landing systems, integrated optics, and digital communications
abstract: For many, 1978 will be remembered as the year the drawn-out battle was won to replace aviation's aging ILS, the instrument landing system that operates on radio frequencies and that was first demonstrated in 1939. The new choice is an MLS (microwave landing system) based on the Time Reference Scanning Beam approach.

articleTitle: Commercial U.S. satellites: A survey of communication satellites, their effect on domestic networks, and a look into the near and long-term future
abstract: Sixteen years ago, when communications via satellite began in earnest, talk of the earth's crowded electromagnetic spectrum was commonplace. Today the radio spectrum available to satellites is becoming similarly crowded, and so is desirable orbit space. It is a measure of the progress in satellite communications since the United States launched Syncom 2. It was the first successful geosynchronous satellite (Fig. 1).

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Keeping tabs on plutonium
abstract: A weak link in protecting against theft of plutonium from storage vaults, according to two University of California computer scientists, is the lack of a monitoring system that could record instantly how much was stolen.

articleTitle: Research and development: The President's R&D budget: Basic is up, applied is not: President Carter asks for more real dollars for basic research, but holds the line in other categories
abstract: The research and development budget that President Carter has proposed for fiscal 1980 calls for a “real” increase — 4 to 5 percent — in Federal outlays for basic research, while spending for applied and developmental research would be maintained at approximately the rate of inflation.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: The science court tested
abstract: When the concept of a science court to resolve disputes over “scientific fact” was endorsed in 1976 by a Presidential task force, we questioned whether it would work (November 1976, p. 29). The task force, part of the Presidential Advisory Group on Anticipated Advances in Science and Technology, suggested that an experiment be set up to test the feasibility of a science court.

articleTitle: The Intelsat 5 generation: Electronics and advanced rocketry have kept pace with long-distance traffic demands to nurture new generation satellites
abstract: Communications satellite technology is paced as much by developments in rocketry as by advances in electronics, and nowhere is this fact as evident as in the Intelsat 5, the latest in a series of international communications satellites. When it came time to freeze the satellite design in 1974, a mix of 11/14-GHz and 4/6-GHz transponders, with provision for interconnections, was chosen. Improvements in the Atlas-Centaur launch vehicle made it possible to add the needed 57. kg to the in-orbit mass of the satellite.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: A different robotic viewpoint
abstract: Fixed TVcameras are old hat on assembly lines for inspection and manipulation. But strapping one on a robot's wrist makes for a different perspective.

articleTitle: Professional concerns: Employment guidelines revisited: A look at the guidelines' second edition; it has been accepted by employers and employees alike
abstract: Six months after its revision and republication, the “Guidelines to Professional Employment for Engineers and Scientists” - a document first published and endorsed by IEEE and 27 other professional societies on Jan. 1, 1973 - has apparently won quiet acceptance by employees and employers alike. This climate of acceptance was predicted in the foreword to the new edition, which was published August 1, 1978. The endorsing societies said in that preface: “They [the guidelines] reflect the combined experience and judgment of many employers and professional employees. The first edition gave credit for the guidelines solely to the endorsing societies.”

articleTitle: Communications: Ten billion bits on a disk: High-power laser diodes and pregrooved disks enable low-cost digital data recording and retrieval
abstract: Compact, high-power laser diode systems should make optical-disk recorders attractive for general office use. Their price/performance ratio will make possible such devices as electronic filing cabinets for electronic mail. For these applications, they have advantages over recently announced optical-disk recorders that employ high-power gas lasers and external modulators. Such recorders of digital information are relatively bulky and expensive and are mainly applicable for mass-storage systems.

articleTitle: Computers: Computing at 4 degrees Kelvin: Superconducting technology and unconventional packaging herald an era of ultrafast, ultrareliable computers
abstract: The Josephson junction, a superconducting device discovered by Brian Josephson in 1962, opens the door to a brand new phase of computer technology. The figures for potential computers based on this new technology stretch the imagination: switching speeds more than ten times faster than today's best machines, with miniature logic that dissipates less than one-thousandth the power of present semiconductor LSI-based devices.

articleTitle: I. `des will be totally insecure within ten years'
abstract: Cryptography. The very name conjures up images of secrecy and spying, with project code names like "Magic" and "Lucifer." And indeed until fairly recently data encryption was a shrouded capability, used almost exclusively by military and diplomatic organizations. The computerization of information processing and transmission has changed this. In response to a growing commercial need, the National Bureau of Standards has promulgated a national Data Encryption Standard, developed by IBM. The standard, called DES, can be implemented in software or on a single LSI chip and can be used with any computer to encrypt and decrypt transmitted data. A single-chip version should sell for about $10 in quantity production. But just how good is the protection offered by DES?

articleTitle: Video-bandwidth compression: a study in tradeoffs
abstract: Image compression is an alluring technology, but so far researchers have found the goal of exploiting it a herculean task. The aim is to narrow the transmitted bandwidth as much as possible. Such compression (Fig. 1) can reduce the cost of transmission for commercial and space applications. It can lessen susceptibility to interference in military missions. But even the most sophisticated compression system results in some loss of image quality, and the higher the compression, the greater the loss. And here lies the problem: In analyzing the compression-clarity tradeoff, researchers have been unable to come up with a generally acceptable way of finding out what constitutes 'adequate' clarity.

articleTitle: Power/Energy: Solar Power Satellites: Microwaves deliver the power: Kilometer-diameter antennas would be used in this super system to transmit power to ground-based rectifying antennas
abstract: The largest, most powerful microwave transmission system ever considered by man has been proposed to deliver the sun's power from space to earth from a network of Solar Power Satellites. The SPS network, with a 5 × 10-km photovoltaic array on each satellite, would convert the sun's energy to electricity prior to transmission.

articleTitle: Computers: The computer speaks: Rapid speech synthesis from printed text input could accommodate an unlimited vocabulary
abstract: As electronic developments go, speech output from a computer is still a novelty; it is being used in isolated applications to teach the blind, educate students in foreign languages and enhance some games. But proponents believe that 10 years of research and the sprinkling of commercial successes have laid the groundwork for major expansion. Computer speech, we believe, should be advancing into the world of business before too long, alongside CRT terminals, line printers, teletypewriters, and the like.

articleTitle: Devices: Visible and UV lasers: Problems and promises: New families of gas lasers are expected to deliver a range of pulse intensities, durations, and wavelengths for diverse applications
abstract: Three new families of powerful and efficient gas lasers — the rare-gas halides, molecular halogens, and mercury halides — all operating in either the ultraviolet or visible regions of the spectrum, are promising candidates for several exciting applications. Unknown several years ago, these new devices — also called excimer lasers — may prove ideal tools for the separation of useful elements from nuclear waste, for laser-driven thermonuclear fusion, for purification of chemical compounds, and for underwater communications and remote sensing of submerged objects.

articleTitle: Nuclear power and the public risk: TMI underscored generic human factors and safety system problems, and challenged the complex art of risk assessment
abstract: The lessons learned from the events leading to the severely damaged core at Three Mile Island's Unit 2 last March 28 point to at least three ways in which the public risk of radioactive exposure from reactors may be decreased without technological breakthroughs. According to documents of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, testimony to the President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island, and almost all specialists interviewed by Spectrum, risk can be lessened by these steps: 1. Improved training for operators on how best to cope with accidents. 2. The upgrading of some reactor safety systems, components, and instruments. 3. Wider planning by utilities and state and Federal agencies on how to protect the public in a nuclear emergency.

articleTitle: Power/energy: First steps to the Solar Power Satellite: Guidelines issued by the Department of Energy and NASA provide a reference point for an ambitious program
abstract: Capturing the sun's awesome energy in space, above the earth's dense, cloudy atmosphere, has been a dream of solar-energy proponents for more than a decade. In the 1960s the success of the space program and the interest in solar energy led to the proposed synergism of solar energy conversion and space technology to send power from space to earth. Thus was born the concept for the Solar Power Satellite (SPS). As conceived, the SPS would convert solar energy to microwaves and beam the energy to collecting antennas on the ground for conversion to usable electricity.

articleTitle: Solid state/computers: Demystifying microprocessor design: Big chips require artful compromises, as demonstrated by this design case history
abstract: Stripped of its mystique, designing a high-performance microprocessor like the Zilog Z8000 is like designing any other complex system of digital electronics, except that good engineering practices, instead of being merely desirable, are crucial. Here are the key rules that the designers of the Z8000 followed:

articleTitle: Innovation: Thomas Edison and his electric lighting system: The inventor's notebooks reveal that he was actually a skilled practitioner of systems engineering, not the tinkerer of legend
abstract: Over the past century no one has better exemplified the image of the heroic inventor than Thomas Alva Edison. What was popularly understood as his “cut and try” approach to invention gave rise to the most prolific inventive career in American history, earned for him the title “the Wizard of Menlo Park” and a place in American folklore. Such imagery, however, is the unfortunate result of much misinformation and conjecture; it has only served to obscure our understanding of a pivotal figure in the history of American technology.

articleTitle: Advanced technology: Digital image processing: Images that provide both high resolution and large dynamic range are transmitted, stored, and processed by digital means
abstract: Digital image processing is helping the U.S. Department of Defense solve problems involving invisible, infrared, synthetic aperture radar, and cartographic data. NASA is applying the technology in remote sensing. Medical applications center on ultrasound and computer-aided tomography. Legal uses involve fingerprints and graphic evidence. Graphics-arts applications include photo composition and four-color printing. And communications uses are in optical character recognition and electronic mail.

The 16-bit 8086 microprocessor introduces to MOS digital design some speed-up techniques well-known to computer architects. Limits on the die size barred these techniques in the past, but with new MOS processes, transistor packing densities are sufficent to use them. As a result, we have been able to design significantly improved performance into the 16-bit 8086 without relying totally on the faster circuits allowed by the new MOS processes.

articleTitle: Power sources: Superbatteries: A progress report: Developers are banking on new materials to drive batteries into a competitive position vis-a-vis oil, gas, and gasoline
abstract: The reign of the lead-acid battery is being threatened by superbatteries that promise to be an important part of the energy scenario toward the end of this century. If present projections hold up, such batteries will help electric utilities meet variations in power demand economically and without pollution of the air. Millions of cars will also likely be powered cleanly by superbatteries.

articleTitle: The technical blow-by-blow: Details of the Three Mile Island accident as excerpted and edited from interviews with Nuclear Regulatory Commission investigators
abstract: Investigators for the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission went to work shortly after the nuclear crisis at Three Mile Island had passed the danger point. Their goal: to establish as accurately as possible the sequence of events that began last March 28 at reactor No. 2.

articleTitle: Aerospace: Microwave sensing from orbit: Enhanced devices penetrate cloud cover to provide data for weather prediction and terrain analysis
abstract: Microwave sensors are emerging as a sensitive and reliable tool for monitoring the earth from satellites. Used in conjunction with the traditional sensors of visible and infrared light, they are extending present capabilities of global weather forecasts and local severe storm watch. Unlike visible or infrared sensors, microwave devices can “see through” clouds. This is a real advantage when one remembers that some regions of the earth, like parts of Venezuela, are nearly always covered with clouds. While cloud pattern is an important part of storm watch, other vital signs — temperature, humidity, and wind fields — must also be monitored. These parameters can be sensed better by microwave devices to give a fuller measure of the strength of a storm or weather front.

articleTitle: Circuit techniques: Enhancing MOS/LSI's role in analog design: High-density amplifiers, A/D and D/A converters, filters, and coder-decoder circuits can now be fabricated
abstract: New design approaches that combine analog and digital functions on one MOS LSI chip are lowering the cost and size and improving the reliability of such circuits as linear amplifiers, AZD and DZA converters, and precision frequency filters. Instead of the conventional multichip and hybrid designs, analog circuits are being fabricated with the same high-density MOS/LSI processes employed for such standard components as digital logic, memory, and microprocessors.

articleTitle: Pascal is a 'natural' [for microprocessor software programs]
abstract: The rapid replacement of hard-wired logic with programmable microprocessors is forcing electronic designers to search for less costly ways of writing, maintaining and updating microprocessor software programs. Most programmers at Texas Instruments feel that writing in a high-level language (HLI) is one effective way to cut costs and that this is particularly true of a language like Pascal, which lends itself to top-down structuring.

articleTitle: Industry: Lasers in the factory: Nd: YAG and CO2 lasers are growing in popularity for cutting, drilling, welding, scribing, and heat-treating a host of metals and nonmetals
abstract: The laser has moved rapidly out of the laboratory, where it is still a research item, onto the factory floor as a production tool. Capable of delivering enormous thermal energy with pinpoint precision at very high speeds, the industrial laser can be found performing a host of material-treatment applications, including surface hardening, cutting, drilling, engraving, welding, material removal and scribing. And the types of materials undergoing laser processing are growing. The list now includes a variety of metals, plastics, rubber, wood, paper, cloth, ceramics, semiconductor materials, and crystals such as diamonds.

articleTitle: Military: particle-beam weapons: a controversy: `highly questionable' is the label applied by four M.I.T. scientists, but the U.S. department of defense is betting on the new scheme
abstract: With just two particle-beam weapon systems installed on satellites in geosynchronous earth orbit at 40000 km, a country could, theoretically, neutralize ICBMs or submarine-launched ballistic missiles fired from any site in the world. Such 'death ray' weapons, it is reported in a study by four physicists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, could - again theoretically - destroy enemy missiles the moment they climbed out of the earth's atmosphere and entered space.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Thermal energy conversion: Tapping the sea depths: Floating energy plants could convert heat stored at different ocean levels to electric power
abstract: Initial studies suggest that the potential for electric energy in ocean thermal gradients off the United States and its islands is on the order of 200 GW. By exploiting these gradients, which occur between different depths of the ocean floor, production plants could convert the solar energy stored as heat in the oceans into continuous electricity. That is the hope of a Federal program called OTEC (for ocean thermal energy conversion).

articleTitle: The decision-makers: A cacophony of voices: The tangle of politics, finance, bureaucracy, and the persuasive arts yields "go no-go" answers for the nuclear industry
abstract: Building a nuclear power plant in the United States is not a job for the faint at heart. It takes a minimum of seven years of planning, studies, reviews, and hearings just to get the Federal, state, and local permits for construction. At least six more years are needed to build the plant and obtain an operating license. That is the quick way to put up a nuclear power plant. In practice, it rarely happens that fast.

articleTitle: Electronic watches: The quartz watch: Its life and times: Intervals between battery replacement will increase as the watch improves in accuracy and versatility
abstract: The rapid advance of the quartz watch in the marketplace is far from leveling off. Of the approximately 280 million watches expected to be sold this year, an estimated 30 percent will be quartz, with the percentage increasing during the 1980s. While the liquid-crystal display (LCD) leads in quartz watch sales, the quartz analog watch is advancing from second place, and quartz watches that use light-emitting-diode (LED) displays are falling behind.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Exploiting wave power: To realize the promise, engineers must deal with unique power-transfer modes, erratic seas, and unfavorable economics
abstract: One of the more promising renewable sources of electric power is ocean waves. And one of the best-placed countries for extracting this power is the United Kingdom. Waves along the Atlantic coast here are among the most energetic in the world. Typically 2-3 m high, these waves have a period of 10 s (a wavelength of 150 m), and on the average they contain between 40 to 90 kW of power for every meter of wave front. With 1000-1500 km of coastline, the U.K.'s potential for wave power is larger than that of any other renewable power resource available to the country.

articleTitle: On Bell: I. Time for a change: A former FCC common carrier bureau chief believes there's a better way to structure the communications industry
abstract: To most persons, “telecommunication” means plain old telephone service; and “information” is an abstract concept with little perceived relationship to telecommunications. The world, however, has entered what many consider to be an “information age,” in which the generation, acquisition processing, exchange, and use of information is becoming more central to social, economic, and political processes than are such well-known activities as farming, manufacturing, and merchandising. Indeed, most of the latter activities would be crippled without extensive information processing and exchange. Telecommunication, including not only plain old telephone service, but also many new forms of voice, data, and image transfer, is an indispensable element in these processes.

Something new happened to microprocessors last year: they became the software equivalent of minicomputers. At least the top of the line did. Instead of the difficult machine-language software that processors once worked with, the new microcomputers can handle the same easier, high-level languages (HLL) that the bigger computers have always used. With a minimum of program fine-tuning, they can execute quickly programs written in assembly or machine code.

articleTitle: Solid State: VLSI: Scoping its future: The experts probe the alternatives among markets, business structures, and resources, as well as technical challenges
abstract: The semiconductor industry's ability to make laboratory VLSI devices is no longer seriously doubted. What to do with those ICS is really the challenge.

articleTitle: New product applications: Winchester fixed disk drive series features 5.3-and 10.7-megabyte unformatted storage capacity
abstract: The 8-in (20.3 cm) Winchester fixed disk drive series offers 5.3 and 10.7 megabytes at a relatively low cost per megabyte.

articleTitle: Hew product applications: Light-polarizing gates provide high linearity for direct-writing analog data recorder
abstract: The HR-2000 Datagraph is a solid-state direct-writing recorder of analog signal information. With a programmable light array, the instrument is able to eliminate problems of linearity, beam deflection, tangential error, overshoot, and torque - all common to conventional galvanometer and CRT recording instruments and devices.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Solar energy: Four sites demonstrate potential: An office building in Florida, a warehouse in New Hampshire, a gymnasium in Iowa, and a laundry in California exploit sun power
abstract: For all the discussion of solar alternatives to fossil fuels, there has been little hard data on performance. Such data is beginning to emerge from operating solar-energy systems installed under the National Solar Heating and Cooling Demonstration Program. I he findings for four systems are particularly interesting because they represent a range of possibilities- hot water, space heating, space cooling — at both newly constructed and retrofitted installations — and include both active and passive designs operating at a broad sweep of sites: in New Hampshire, Florida, California, and Iowa.

Dynamic connection of beams on board a satellite raises the prospect of “central offices” in the sky that could route signals to their destinations on earth via separate spacecraft antenna beams. On-board switching would eliminate almost all of the terrestrial transmission and switching now needed.

articleTitle: Applications literature: Microcomputer hardware and software explained
abstract: Here is a 20-page catalog giving current information on the TRS-80 microcomputer, its peripherals and accessories, application ideas, and detailed specifications. A general section in the catalog explains what a microcomputer is, what it can do, who can use it, etc. The text also describes the TRS-80 Level-I and Level-II Basic language.

A decade of scientific effort was reaching its climax while the world watched on television. It was, as the astronauts said in that moment of history, just -one small step for a man,-but its impact will be felt down the ages to the final moment of mankind. It may even be that in the very distant future, out of the maelstrom of our chaotic century, only that epochal event will be remembered and the name of the United States immortalized by it alone.

abstract: Barney designed low-drift operational amplifiers until integrated circuits came along. Now that quality op amps are available on a chip, Barney is looking for a job.

articleTitle: Aerospace: Planning Space Shuttle's maiden voyage: In a matter of months space-oriented experiments will soar aloft aboard the Columbia
abstract: A quantum leap toward mankind's use of space as a natural resource begins with the first orbital flight of the Space Shuttle. The test flight, now scheduled for early next year, will mark the first time a satellite was orbited without use of an expendable booster. As future flights unfold — and 500 are planned in the first 12 years — the Shuttle will give the world routine, round-trip access to space. Capable of flying both in air and space, the Shuttle represents the highest technical achievement of the U.S. space program.

articleTitle: Transportation. The LIRR: A system riding troubled tracks: Will the aggravations of its 100 000 commuters ever end? You are invited to help the railroad solve its problems
abstract: “Did you know that when you die you've got to change in Jamaica to get where you're going?” a Long Island Rail Road commuter said to the man standing next to him in the car's crowded aisle. The train was already three minutes late pulling out of New York's Pennsylvania Station, and the heating system wasn't working. Running through the minds of their fellow commuters were visions of trains stuck in the tunnel, and cold meals upon reaching home.

William Girdner was a 24-year-old electrical engineer in 1939 when he attended a meeting of the Institute of Radio Engineers in San Francisco at which Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard spoke about the new audio oscillator they were producing in the now-famous garage behind the Packard home in Palo Alto, Calif. Excited by "the best grasp of the industry's future of anyone I had ever heard," Girdner wasted no time asking for a job. On April 1, 1939, he became the third employee of the business, reporting for work shortly after it had moved out of the garage into a small building on Page Mill Road behind Tinker Bell's Fixit Shop. Girdner remembers Hewlett's and Packard's management philosophy from the start. It was more than just an informal, first-name style. It involved standing back as far as possible and letting people solve their own problems.

articleTitle: Assessing the new services: Political and legal issues will impact implementation of broadband digital transmission
abstract: Mature digital technology and a regulatory environment that favors competition are making possible the development of radically new communications facilities and services for businesses in the United States, starting in 1981-84. Already competition is under way between companies offering such large systems as Satellite Business Systems (SBS), AT&T's Advanced Communication Service (ACS), and the Xerox Corp.'s Telecommunications Network (XTEN), though the capabilities they would offer are still in the proposal stage.

articleTitle: New product applications: Real-time measurement and control system with keyboard and CRT features integral sensor I/O
abstract: “Macsym II” is a user-programmable, self-contained system that provides automated real-time measurement and control in a variety of laboratory and processing applications. Priced from $5600 in 50-piece quantities ($6990 in single quantities) for a basic machine, the system processes high- and low-level analog signals from sensors such as thermocouples, strain gauges, and resistive-temperature devices.

articleTitle: New product applications: 12-MHz single- and dual-trace oscilloscopes are the smallest professional-grade instruments
abstract: “Mini” oscilloscopes that operate at 12 MHz are offered in dual-trace (model 1022A - $785) and single-trace (1021A - $595) versions. Both are completely portable, yet offer a 4×5-cm screen. The series provides sweep rates from 100 ns/division to 100 ms/division in 12 calibrated steps. A variable ×10 magnifier is standard.

articleTitle: New product applications: Total 16-bit A/D converter is offered in a single 32-pin dual-in-line package
abstract: The MN5280 is the first 16-pin successive-approximation A/D converter in a dual-in-line package. It is designed as a low-cost, physically small alternative to modular and PC-card high-resolution A/D converters. Dimensions are 1.72 by 1.12 by 0.39 in., including pin height (4.37 by 2.85 by 0.99 cm).

articleTitle: New product applications: Universal development system supports all popular 8-bit microprocessor systems
abstract: The AMDS-AFD microcomputer development system provides ail the tools needed for product design and testing of a wide range of popular microprocessors, including the Models 8080, 8085, 6800, 6802, and Z80. The system station includes the CPU (with choice of processor and 48 kbytes of static RAM), a universal logic analyzer, the CRT, and the keyboard.

articleTitle: New product applications: 1-GHz bandwidth, highest so far, achieved in a laboratory oscilloscope
abstract: The Model 7104 general-purpose laboratory plug-in oscilloscope sets new standards of performance with its 1-GHz bandwidth and 20-cm/ns writing rate. The instrument also features a horizontal (x-y) bandwidth of dc to 350 MHz, rise time of 350 ps, and calibrated sweep speeds up to 200 ps/division. Vertical sensitivity ranges from 10 mV to 1 V per division.

articleTitle: New product applications: Low-price, portable, 3 1/2-digit multimeters designed for a wide range of applications
abstract: Five new 3 1/2-digit portable multimeters with low price tags have been designed for a wide range of applications. Three models - the 3010, 3020, and RMS-3030 - are for use by engineers, technicians, and service representatives. Two models - the TECH-300 and TECH-310 - are for technicians and hobbyists. All feature 10-A ac/dc ranges (not available on the Model TECH-300), two-year battery life, a semiconductor test function, and overload protection on all ranges. A quick continuity test function (not available on the Model TECH-300) enables users to measure continuity with the speed of an analog volt-ohm meter.

Smaller than the traditional dual in-line package (DIP), the quad in-line package (QUIP) allows a much larger, higher density, faster device to be packaged. The manufacturer says that the 64-pin QUIP is also superior to the 40-pin DIPS generally used to package microprocessrs and to the 68-pin square package. The new package can be used efficiently on both low-cost, two-sided wiring boards and on multilayer boards.
